nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Silver Jenny
Scientific Name: Eucinostomus gula

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class : Osteichthys
      Order: Perciformes
      Family: Gerreidae

Other Common Names: common mojarra (581); mojarra (312); Irish pompano (834); sand perch, mutton minnow (664); jenny mojarra (791)

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (956)
Other: Taxonomic note.  Matheson and McEachran (1444) separated Eucinostomus harengulus Goode and Bean from the E. argenteus complex. Robins et a1 (956) recognized this distinction and included E. harengulus, the tidewater mojarra, as a separate species in the 1991 Common and Scientific Names list. It is probable that earlier studies of E. gula and E. argenteus included specimens of the now recognized E. harengulus.

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Not harvested or exploited commercially throughout most of its range (312 834). In the Caribbean it is marketed fresh in many localities although it is not highly esteemed (791). Caught mainly with beach seines, but also with gillnets, trammel nets, beam trawls, traps, and cast nets (791).

Recreational: Limited value as a bait fish (871).

Ecological Role: Important as a forage species because of its abundance. Known to be preyed upon by gray snappers in Florida Bay (724).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Distributed from Massachusetts to Argentina including Bermuda and throughout the Gulf of Mexico (791 834 871 891), although it occurs only as a straggler north of Beaufort, NC (312 834). Common on the Florida west coast (378 581 664). Also found offshore in the Gulf of Mexico (833).

Within Study Area: Found in shallow estuarine waters throughout Florida (891). One of the most common species of the Charlotte Harbor area (789). Reported as the second most abundant species near Flamingo, Everglades National Park comprising almost 24% of the total fish catch (1373). Eucinostomus spp. is among the dominant species in the Ten Thousand Islands area (1054 1263 1443). E. gula was the most abundant species overall in studies of Florida Bay conducted by Sogard et al (851 852). Sogard et a1 (851 1243 1432) found that greater densities of Eucinostomus spp. (primarily E. gula) occurred in western Florida Bay than in other portions of the bay although they were taken throughout the bay. Thayer and Chester (1431) and Thayer et a1 (724) reported E. gula as the second most abundant species of fish collected in Florida Bay with trawls (27.4% of catch) and block nets. Eucinostomus spp. was the ninth most abundant fish taxon collected with throw traps in Florida Bay (1243).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: E. gula exhibit a diurnal pattern of activity in response to tidal stage or other factors, and increased numbers occur on the mudbanks in Florida Bay at dawn and dusk (852 1432). Low (1179), however, caught E. gula primarily at mid-day in Biscayne Bay. May occur in small schools (791) .

nodes.title: Movements/Migrations
nodes.body: The adults migrate to offshore waters as winter approaches, and following spawning, the young migrate inshore to estuarine waters during the summer and early fall (378 581 664 1361).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Found in shallow saltwater and brackish water habitats (702 791), but uncommon in freshwater (790). Abundant along sandy shorelines (871). Inhabit deeper flats and sloping sides of shallow flats in areas of sparse vegetation (581). Often associated with seagrass beds, dense algae and mangrove prop roots (664 724 789 871 1243 1422). Known to occur in freshwater in the Caloosahatchee River (265), the Indian River area (848), and the Shark River and North River in southwest Florida (395 515 1043). Taken offshore in the Gulf of Mexico at depths of 7.5 to 67m (303 833).

Substrate: Smaller individuals are found in areas densely vegetated with algae (664 789). Collected over mud bottoms and over oyster bars (1445). Especially abundant over mud bottoms in mangrove-lined creeks and lagoons, but also found over vegetated sand bottoms (791). Sogard et a1 (1243) found the species most abundant over mixed seagrass beds containing Halodule, Thalassia and Syringodium. Also collected in areas of sparse vegetation (581), over rock bottoms (363), and over clean, sandy bottoms (363 1445). Thayer et a1 (724) reported approximately equal numbers of E. gula collected in mangrove prop roots and over seagrass beds. nodes.body: Juvenile/adults: Collected in Florida at temperatures of 7.2-32.3 C at Cedar Key (581), 12.8-32.5 C in Tampa Bay (664), 16-34 C in Everglades National Park (702 1373); 19.9-33.6 C at Matecumbe Key (800), and 18-36 C at Jupiter Inlet (887).

nodes.title: Salinity

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title: Silver Jenny (Eucinostomus gula)

FLELMR CODE: 1673

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name:  Silver Jenny
Scientific Name: Eucinostomus gula

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class : Osteichthys
      Order: Perciformes
      Family: Gerreidae

Other Common Names: common mojarra (581); mojarra (312); Irish pompano (834); sand perch, mutton minnow (664); jenny mojarra (791)

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (956)
Other: Taxonomic note.  Matheson and McEachran (1444) separated Eucinostomus harengulus Goode and Bean from the E. argenteus complex. Robins et a1 (956) recognized this distinction and included E. harengulus, the tidewater mojarra, as a separate species in the 1991 Common and Scientific Names list. It is probable that earlier studies of E. gula and E. argenteus included specimens of the now recognized E. harengulus.

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Not harvested or exploited commercially throughout most of its range (312 834). In the Caribbean it is marketed fresh in many localities although it is not highly esteemed (791). Caught mainly with beach seines, but also with gillnets, trammel nets, beam trawls, traps, and cast nets (791).

Recreational: Limited value as a bait fish (871).

Ecological Role: Important as a forage species because of its abundance. Known to be preyed upon by gray snappers in Florida Bay (724).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Distributed from Massachusetts to Argentina including Bermuda and throughout the Gulf of Mexico (791 834 871 891), although it occurs only as a straggler north of Beaufort, NC (312 834). Common on the Florida west coast (378 581 664). Also found offshore in the Gulf of Mexico (833).

Within Study Area: Found in shallow estuarine waters throughout Florida (891). One of the most common species of the Charlotte Harbor area (789). Reported as the second most abundant species near Flamingo, Everglades National Park comprising almost 24% of the total fish catch (1373). Eucinostomus spp. is among the dominant species in the Ten Thousand Islands area (1054 1263 1443). E. gula was the most abundant species overall in studies of Florida Bay conducted by Sogard et al (851 852). Sogard et a1 (851 1243 1432) found that greater densities of Eucinostomus spp. (primarily E. gula) occurred in western Florida Bay than in other portions of the bay although they were taken throughout the bay. Thayer and Chester (1431) and Thayer et a1 (724) reported E. gula as the second most abundant species of fish collected in Florida Bay with trawls (27.4% of catch) and block nets. Eucinostomus spp. was the ninth most abundant fish taxon collected with throw traps in Florida Bay (1243).

Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content: E. gula exhibit a diurnal pattern of activity in response to tidal stage or other factors, and increased numbers occur on the mudbanks in Florida Bay at dawn and dusk (852 1432). Low (1179), however, caught E. gula primarily at mid-day in Biscayne Bay. May occur in small schools (791) .

sections.heading: Movements/Migrations
sections.content: The adults migrate to offshore waters as winter approaches, and following spawning, the young migrate inshore to estuarine waters during the summer and early fall (378 581 664 1361).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type: Found in shallow saltwater and brackish water habitats (702 791), but uncommon in freshwater (790). Abundant along sandy shorelines (871). Inhabit deeper flats and sloping sides of shallow flats in areas of sparse vegetation (581). Often associated with seagrass beds, dense algae and mangrove prop roots (664 724 789 871 1243 1422). Known to occur in freshwater in the Caloosahatchee River (265), the Indian River area (848), and the Shark River and North River in southwest Florida (395 515 1043). Taken offshore in the Gulf of Mexico at depths of 7.5 to 67m (303 833).

Substrate: Smaller individuals are found in areas densely vegetated with algae (664 789). Collected over mud bottoms and over oyster bars (1445). Especially abundant over mud bottoms in mangrove-lined creeks and lagoons, but also found over vegetated sand bottoms (791). Sogard et a1 (1243) found the species most abundant over mixed seagrass beds containing Halodule, Thalassia and Syringodium. Also collected in areas of sparse vegetation (581), over rock bottoms (363), and over clean, sandy bottoms (363 1445). They suggested that the presence of large numbers of young E. gula in the prop roots implied that the roots provided refuge for the young fish, and that this was an important habitat for growth and survival of the species (724) .
